newsitem.title: UK: British writer seeks reward on Nazi gold-raid book.
newsitem.headline: British writer seeks reward on Nazi gold-raid book.

text.p: A new book asserting that commandos smuggled Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler's close aide Martin Bormann into Britain brought a 20,000 pound ($31,760) reward challenge on literary agents Curtis Brown on Friday.

The book "Operation James Bond", which purports to be a real-life cloak-and-dagger saga involving Nazi gold, provoked controversy last month by saying Bormann was brought here in 1945 on wartime prime minister Winston Churchill's orders.
It suggests that British commandos staged a raid into Berlin, as the Red Army closed in, to seize Bormann and get his signature on documents releasing Nazi gold held by Swiss banks.
Author Christopher Creighton's work was disputed by another writer, Ian Sayer who claimed a reward offered by the agents for anyone who could disprove the book's theme.
Bormann stayed close to Hitler till the last days of the Third Reich but virtually alone among the top Nazi leaders his fate remained unknown after the war.

Some historians suggest he was killed by Russian snipers in a mass breakout from Hitler's chancellory in the ruins of Berlin. He was sentenced to death in his absence by the Nuremberg War Crimes Tribunal in 1946.
Creighton has insisted he was second-in-command of a 300-strong commando unit led by James Bond creator Ian Fleming that saved Bormann from the gallows.
He said the commando team spirited Bormann, who was responsible for Hitler's finances, out of Berlin to help release Nazi gold stored in Swiss banks.
The book met with such scepticism that Curtis Brown, which acts for Creighton, issued a challenge with advertisements in national newspapers this week.
They offered a 20,000 pound reward to anyone who could "provide evidence that Operation James Bond did not take place".
The challenge was taken up by author Sayer, who in 1984 wrote a book on the subject, titled "Nazi Gold".
Today he sent in his claims to Curtis Brown asking that the reward money be given to charities for families and survivors of the Nazi Holocaust.

Sayer said he had proof that Creighton and the Bormann rescue team could not have travelled on a Wellington bomber of 161 Squadron in April, 1945, as the book claims. He also said he had found around 120 factual inaccuracies in the book.
"I have documentary evidence that the 161 Squadron did not operate Wellington bombers in 1945," Sayer told Reuters.

Sayer also said he had done extensive research on gold plundered by the Nazis from occupied European countries during World War Two and claimed it would not have been necessary for Churchill to have Bormann smuggled out of Germany.

"Bormann would not have any access to the Nazi gold," Sayer said adding that he had documentary evidence that the Swiss government had frozen Nazi assets in Swiss banks in February 1945 - three months before the alleged Bormann rescue.
"Bormann would not have been able to get his hands on the gold," Sayer said.
Creighton, a former television and film director, said the book may contain some "minor" inaccuracies but was adamant that the rescue did take place.
"Twentytwo of us flew in a Wellington in April 1945 and rescued Bormann. I was there - it happened," he said.
No-one at Curtis Brown was immediately available to comment.
German authorities said Bormann's remains were found in December, 1972 in Berlin.
Creighton said Bormann was flown to Argentina in 1956 and died in Paraguay in 1959.
He said the remains were taken back to Berlin under a deal involving the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency, the Paraguayan government and German intelligence. $1=.6298 Pound)
